title: Polar Bear Walk
role: CREATURE ANIMATION / AI VIDEO MOCAP / FUR + LOOK DEVELOPMENT
description: A polar bear walk cycle captured from an AI video: a generated clip of my own model, fitted to a Blender rig and rebuilt as a clean looping walk, then groomed, lit on arctic snow and pushed to photoreal footage with LTX-2.5.

videos.title: Polar Bear Walk, final shot (10 seconds)

body: ## Human + Claude

This polar bear was never animated by hand, and I never opened Blender to make it. The walk is motion capture from an AI video: a generated clip of my own model walking, turned into a clean, looping walk cycle on a real rig. Everything after that, the fur, the snow, the light and the final photoreal pass, was built on top of that walk.

My only interface was a conversation with Claude Code, running Anthropic's Opus 5.5. Claude wrote and ran every script in Blender, Houdini and ComfyUI on my workstation. My part was the one I know from years of VFX work: looking at every take and saying what was wrong with it.
## The Idea

The idea is simple to say: render your own model from the side, let a video model make it walk, then copy that video back onto the skeleton. I wanted to do it with MiniMax H3 running locally in ComfyUI, on a Tripo polar bear, and push it far past game quality.
## A Mesh That Can Walk

The Tripo model looked good and was useless for rigging. The head was turned off-axis, left and right did not match, and the hind paws floated 3.5 cm above the ground. Claude straightened the neck along its measured midline, made the body symmetric, rebuilt the surface in Houdini as 16,000 clean quads, made new UVs and transferred the original texture across.
![Before and after: the head straightened and the body made symmetric](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/mesh-symmetry.webp)
![The rebuilt mesh: 16k quads from Houdini Quad Remesh](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/mesh-wireframe.webp)

The rig is built from code as well: IK paws that live in world space so a planted paw can never slide, toes that bend at the right joint, separate claws, and corrective smoothing on the joints. When I spotted the paws creasing, the skinning was redone and the hind paws learned to curl like the front ones.
::video[Rig deformation test: walk extremes on the left legs](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/rig-deformation.mp4)
::video[Paw skinning before and after, half speed](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/paw-skinning.mp4)
## The Reference

A video model needs a picture it cannot misread. The bear was rendered in its rest pose from the side and from the front at once, on chroma green, with the left lower legs painted pink and the right ones blue so the legs can be told apart later.
![The two-view input frame: side and front, legs colour-coded](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/h3-input.webp)

MiniMax H3 turned that single frame into 192 frames of the bear walking on the spot. It is a treadmill walk: the body stays in place while the planted paws slide back at walking speed. One clip holds about two and a half usable cycles of 58 frames each, and the motion has what I wanted: weight, shoulders and hips that work, and paws that drag and flick.
::video[The MiniMax H3 reference: 192 generated frames, side and front](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/h3-reference.mp4)
## From Video To Bones

This is where most of the first day went, and most of it went wrong. Fitting the rig to the video frame by frame gave jitter and broken poses. Tracing paw paths into a procedural walk was smooth and dead. A hand-keyed walk was snappy and had no weight. Copying the fitted rotations straight onto the rig popped the knees on every step. I rejected all of them, loudly.

What finally worked has two halves. First, fit one periodic cycle to all the video cycles at once. Every bone gets a smooth repeating curve, a small differentiable renderer draws the rig into both views, and an optimiser moves the curves until the silhouette and the pink and blue legs sit on the video. Because it is one cycle averaged over the whole clip, the noise cancels and the result loops by construction. It takes about five minutes on one GPU and lands at 94% silhouette overlap from the side and 95% from the front.
::video[The fit: H3 reference, fitted rig through the same cameras, and the rig outline over the reference](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/fit-overlay.mp4)

Second, rebuild the walk from that fit instead of transferring it. The body keeps the fitted motion, symmetrised and smoothed, with the head held level. The legs are built fresh, using the fit as a guide: exact planted contacts, a heel-first strike, a continuous swing between them, and overlapping action on the paws and toes so they trail the leg and flick through.
::video[Paws against the reference, half speed](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/paws-vs-h3.mp4)
## Directing The Walk

A walk that passes its checks is not yet a good walk. It took 14 rebuilds, each answering one note. The hind paws had to roll like the front ones. A strange slowdown appeared whenever a front paw landed; fixing it lost the feeling of weight; fixing that flattened the shoulders and made the head bob. The version I approved lets the shoulder blades turn about their middle, with the chest hanging between them, which is how a bear carries its weight.
::video[Shoulders and head against the reference, half speed](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/shoulders-vs-h3.mp4)
Every build was checked on a ground plane before I saw it: nothing below the ground, no joint pops, no jitter, knees never locked, the head steady.
::video[The approved walk, three-quarter view on a ground plane](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/walk-three-quarter.mp4)
::video[The approved walk from a low paw camera](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/walk-paw-cam.mp4)
## Seventy-Six Versions Of Fur

The fur is Blender hair curves built with geometry nodes and rendered in Cycles. It started badly: a real-time attempt, then a bear that looked bald, then one that looked puffy, as if it had come straight from the dry cleaner. The fix was to stop guessing and study photographs of real polar bears region by region: hair length, how strongly it clumps, how far it lifts off the skin, where it hangs.
![Six of the groom versions on the way](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/fur-progression.webp)
Those measurements became maps painted over the body that drive the groom.
![Groom maps: length, clumping, lift, wave and the hanging belly fringe](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/fur-groom-maps.webp)

The direction of the hair got its own study, section by section, after I pointed out the flow had been mapped wrong. Later rounds added the stray hairs that break up the outline of the legs and back, the wet yellowish fringe under the belly, toe tufts around the claws, and a nose pad that reads as skin instead of plastic.
![Detail views of the groom: head, nape, legs and paws](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/fur-detail-views.webp)
## Golden Hour On The Ice

For the shot I gave Claude one photograph of a polar bear in low golden light and asked for that. The camera was matched to it, and the sun direction was solved from the lit and shadowed sides of the bear: low from the left, two degrees above the horizon. The first attempt had it mirrored, and I caught it.

The snow took the longest, more than 300 look-development renders. Sculpted terrain kept reading as a flat plain or as lumps. What worked was building it in the material: layered noises for wind-packed drifts, mixed with scanned snow textures, with fine crust added only in patches. Each round was measured against the photograph, down to how much of the frame sits in blue shadow.
![The fur in the shot lighting, rendered in Cycles](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/fur-final-closeup.webp)
::video[The Cycles render: follow camera with a subtle handheld move, film grain](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/cg-walk.mp4)
## From CG To Footage

The last step uses the CG shot as a blueprint for a video model. ChatGPT repainted the first CG frame as a photoreal frame, keeping the bear, the light and the drifts where they were. Then LTX-2.5 with a Layout-to-Render control LoRA generated the clip: the CG video drives the camera and the bear's motion, and the photoreal frame sets the look. Drag across the same frame below, from the Cycles render to the repainted frame to the generated footage.
::embed[breakdown]
All 241 frames come out in a single pass in about six minutes. The camera move, the handheld wobble and the walk stay locked to the CG, while the model redraws the fur and snow.
::video[The CG layout beside the LTX-2.5 result](assets/projects/polar-bear-walk/cg-vs-ltx.mp4)
## What I Learned

An AI video is a good source of motion and a bad source of animation. The clip had the weight and the life, but it only became usable once it was rebuilt with the rules an animator would apply: clean contacts, heel-first steps, overlap, a steady head. The numbers caught the pops and the sliding; they never caught a walk that simply felt wrong. That part stayed with me.
Claude turned the whole process into a written manual and a reusable skill afterwards, so the next creature starts from the pipeline that worked.

title: F1R - Fugi Visualizer
role: AI MUSIC PROJECT / CODEX / ASCII VISUALIZER
description: F1R is my AI-based music and character art project. This page focuses on the Fugi lyric visualizer I built with Codex: a live browser transmission with an animated ASCII face, audio-reactive motion, synced lyric glitches, and F1R character explorations.
body: ## Project Signal

F1R is the band/project name for an AI-based music and visual identity experiment. `Fugi` is one track inside that world, and the lyric visualizer is only one output from a larger character-driven art direction: music generation, cyberpunk portrait experiments, browser animation, and a fictional hacked transmission language.
The live version is here: [open the Fugi visualizer](https://lilbadger.github.io/fugi-vizualizer/).
![F1R - Fugi live visualizer capture](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/fugi-visualizer-03-glitch.png)
## What I Made With Codex

I used Codex as a build partner to turn the Suno track into a browser-native lyric video. The page is not a rendered video file: it draws the performance live with HTML Canvas, a source portrait, timed lyric cues, procedural glitch cards, and audio-driven motion.

The important part is the workflow. I could describe an idea in motion-design language, inspect what the browser was doing, push the code toward a stronger image, and keep iterating until the piece felt less like a tech demo and more like a tiny F1R transmission.
## Reference To ASCII
![Reference portrait used for the ASCII face](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/reference-tongue-in.png)

The visualizer converts this portrait into an ASCII signal. The browser crops the head, rejects most of the flat blue background, samples color and brightness into character cells, then gives the face a fake depth model so it can yaw, push, trail, and tear with the song.
## Effect Stack
![Fugi effect stack](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/fugi-effect-stack.svg)

The signal chain is intentionally direct: song plus portrait go in; the browser generates the ASCII face, motion, trails, scanlines, HUD noise, and lyric bursts in real time. Codex helped iterate the canvas architecture, timing data, and visual system quickly enough that the tool started feeling more like a live instrument than a static page.
## ASCII Face Layers
![ASCII layer breakdown](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/fugi-ascii-layers.svg)

The portrait is cropped into a face-focused signal, sampled into a character grid, rebuilt as a colored ASCII texture, then pushed through a fake depth model. Audio bands drive the face yaw, pitch, push, trails, and glitch density so the head feels like it is reacting to the track instead of just looping.
reference portrait
-> crop + head mask
-> luminance cells
-> dense/sparse ASCII characters
-> sampled color texture
-> column depth parallax
-> audio-reactive push / yaw / trails
-> lyric glitch overlays
## Why It Matters

This is the kind of AI art project I want to keep expanding: generated music, generated identity, code, timing, motion design, and web-native performance all meeting inside one object. The Fugi lyric video is a small part of F1R, but it proves the pipeline can make a song feel like a character, an interface, and a world.
## F1R Character Explorations
![F1R character glitch portrait](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/f1r-character-glitch.png)
This glitch portrait sits closest to the final visualizer language: neon rabbit mask, blue hacked interface, anonymous user readouts, and a noisy signal texture around the face.
![F1R cinematic real-world look](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/f1r-character-real.png)

The wider cinematic look explores how the F1R character could exist in a real city environment: wet pavement, Bucharest-night energy, long-exposure light trails, and the rabbit mask treated as a diegetic neon device.
![F1R building-face character exploration](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/f1r-character-building-face.png)

This version pushes the identity into a stranger direction, turning the face into architecture. It is not just a portrait variation; it suggests that F1R could be a person, a place, a broadcast, or an infected city surface.
## Extended Video Tests

After the browser visualizer was working, I started testing how the F1R language could move outside the ASCII interface. One direction was Seedance 2.0: I was experimenting with ways to generate shots that feel longer than the usual short AI-video fragment, trying to keep the motion connected enough that it can read as a bigger sequence instead of a disconnected clip.
::video[Seedance 2.0 long-form motion test](https://youtu.be/gLuIE9k17i8)

I also tested LTX locally, looking for the best quality I could get from a local video-generation setup. The differences can be subtle; after a point, the choice becomes less about one tool being magically better and more about budget, render time, hardware, control, and how much cleanup a shot can survive.
::video[LTX local video quality test](https://youtu.be/XBlEapUXuz4)
## High Resolution Illustration Studies

These stills explore the F1R world as higher-resolution illustrations rather than realtime browser graphics. The process mixed ChatGPT image work with local image models for cleanup and upscaling, then Photoshop color adjustments to pull the final frames closer to the same neon, wet, hacked-signal mood.
![F1R high resolution illustration study v003](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/f1r-highres-illustration-study-v003.png)
![F1R high resolution illustration study v004](assets/projects/fugi-visualizer/f1r-highres-illustration-study-v004.png)

title: Night of the Living Dead - LTX-2 Contest
description: For an LTX-2 contest, I rebuilt a complete sequence from Night of the Living Dead as generated footage while keeping the supplied soundtrack and editorial duration fixed so the result could drop back into the film.
body: ## The Constraint

The contest started with one sequence from the 1968 film `Night of the Living Dead`. I could redesign every image, but the supplied audio and the 108.885-second editorial duration had to remain the spine of the piece. The generated shots therefore had to land on the existing performances, cuts, pauses, and sound cues closely enough for the replacement sequence to fit back into the full movie.
![Original source sequence frame](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/original-scene-frame.jpg)

I split the scene into a shot-by-shot package and carried the original timing through the whole workflow. The archive eventually grew into 22 working shot folders, each holding experiments, structural passes, restyles, composites, motion generations, and selects. That organization mattered because this was not one hero shot; it was a continuous edit that had to survive from first frame to last.
## Structure Before Style

Before asking an image model for a new world, I extracted controls from the source. HED edges held onto silhouettes and important object boundaries, while depth passes gave the restyle and motion stages a stronger understanding of foreground, background, and spatial separation.
![HED edge guide extracted from the source shot](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/structure-hed.png)
![Depth guide used to preserve the shot layout](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/structure-depth.png)
These guides were not treated as finished images. They were constraints: enough structure to preserve the shot, but enough freedom for the generated sequence to become a different visual world.
## Qwen Look Development

I used Qwen Image Edit inside ComfyUI for the main restyle stage. Multi-reference conditioning let me push a consistent graphic direction across different source shots, while prompt iterations and a Lightning LoRA made it practical to test variations quickly. I was looking for a sickly green and cyan broadcast-horror language built around CRT screens, hard comic shading, and exaggerated characters.
![Qwen Image Edit restyle iteration](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/qwen-restyle.png)
![Upscaled composite prepared for motion generation](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/qwen-composite.png)

The restyle alone was rarely enough. I combined and upscaled selected elements so faces, screens, props, and silhouettes were stable before motion generation. That gave LTX-2 a cleaner starting image and reduced the amount of repair needed after each pass.
## From Still To Motion

For motion I worked with LTX-2 19B through several controlled paths rather than relying on a single image-to-video prompt. Pose, canny, depth, image conditioning, and audio conditioning could be mixed according to what a shot needed. Short tests helped me diagnose motion before committing to longer generations.
::video[LTX-2 pose-guided motion test](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/wip-ltx-pose.mp4)

DWPose was especially useful when the source performance had readable body language that needed to survive the redesign. For crowded shots I assembled a more stable multi-character image first, then used that composite as the motion source.
![DWPose guide for a multi-character source shot](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/dwpose-guide.png)
![Multi-character composite before LTX-2 generation](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/multi-character-composite.png)
## Audio-Guided Takes

The original soundtrack was more than a delivery requirement: it also became a conditioning signal. Audio-guided LTX-2 passes helped movement and performance energy respond to the existing dialogue and rhythm while I kept the source edit locked.
::video[Selected audio-guided shot experiment](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/wip-audio-guided-shot.mp4)

The multi-character shots needed more iteration because consistency, eyelines, action, and screen direction all had to work at once. This selected WIP shows the point where the generated motion began to behave like part of a sequence rather than an isolated AI clip.
::video[Multi-character audio-guided LTX-2 take](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/wip-multi-character-shot.mp4)
## ComfyUI Graph

This is the compact LTXV setup I used for one of the selected shots. Two prepared image states are preprocessed and supplied as first/last-frame controls, while a trimmed section of the source audio drives the generation. The central settings group keeps the LTX-2 checkpoint, distilled/detail/camera-control LoRAs, prompt, 1432 x 1088 output size, 153-frame length, 24 fps, seed, CFG, and steps visible in one place before Video Combine writes the result.
![ComfyUI LTXV first-last-frame and audio workflow](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/comfyui-ltx2-pose-workflow.png)
## Camera And Shot Design

I also tested camera reinterpretations instead of tracing every source frame literally. Close, wide, side, aerial, and low-angle prompts let me look for a more authored shot while still respecting the editorial function of the original beat.
![Low-angle camera variation from the look-development stage](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/camera-low-angle.png)
## Editorial Reintegration

The final stage was selection and repair: choose the strongest generations, reject motion that broke continuity, check cut points against the fixed soundtrack, and assemble the sequence at 24 fps in Blender. I preserved the canonical final export's audio stream in the web version above.
![Final sequence frame - CRT carried through the doorway](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/final-frame-doorway.jpg)
![Final sequence frame - ensemble confrontation](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/final-frame-ensemble.jpg)
![Final sequence frame - broadcast presenter close-up](assets/projects/night-of-the-living-dead-ltx-contest/final-frame-presenter.jpg)
## What I Learned

Long-form generated video is mainly a continuity problem. A beautiful single shot is easy to admire and easy to replace; a sequence has to preserve timing, character identity, eyelines, screen direction, action, and the intention of every cut. The strongest workflow was not one model or one prompt. It was a controlled loop between source analysis, restyle, motion tests, repair, and editorial judgment.

title: F1R - Fugi Live
role: AI MUSIC VIDEO / POINT-CLOUD PERFORMANCE / CUDA PIPELINE
description: A full-length music video for F1R's song Fugi: an LTX-2.3 singing performance rebuilt as an audio-reactive 3D point cloud, filmed by a virtual handheld camera that can circle the singer.

videos.title: F1R - Fugi (live point performance), full music video

body: ## The Brief

F1R is my AI music and character project. `Fugi` is one of its songs, the same track behind my [Fugi lyric visualizer](/projects/fugi-visualizer/). For the live version I wanted a full-length music video in which the singer never stops performing, yet the camera is free to leave the flat video frame: drift around her, move behind her, pull back and come in close, all driven by the song.

The starting point was a 10-second live-performance clip of the F1R singer, neon rabbit mask and all, and the 4:37 Romanian master. The final film runs 6,660 frames at 24 fps: a singing performance rebuilt as dense, glowing, ordered points inside a 3D network of hearts and signal pulses.
![Original live-performance source frame](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/source-live-frame.jpg)
## Routes That Failed First

The approved look came out of a long run of rejected versions, and the rejections shaped it as much as the approvals did. The first layered versions used depth passes and SYSTMS TimeSlice cells to hide the seam of a 237-frame loop; they worked, but they were still a flat video with effects on top. A single-frame RGB-D and Gaussian route looked like cardboard the moment the camera moved. A Vista4D whole-video reconstruction produced real points but only allowed a narrow, cautious orbit.

The version that finally worked, and that I approved as the concept, combined a natively generated singing performance, video-based reconstruction, discrete volumetric points and a handheld camera reacting to the music. From there the full song went through nearly 90 more review versions before the final master.
## Singing Performance With LTX-2.3

Because the song is 4:37 long, the performance had to be generated, not looped. I separated the vocals with Demucs and used the exact vocal-stem interval for each section to drive LTX-2.3 audio-to-video, so the lips, jaw, breathing and head movement follow the Romanian lyrics.

The song was covered by 28 overlapping tiles of 321 frames each. Every tile advances 10 seconds and keeps 81 frames of shared handle. Adjacent tiles share one boundary keyframe: tile N ends on key N+1 and tile N+1 starts from it. The keys were ImageGen variations of one approved frame, held to under about 3 degrees of head turn so identity, mask, microphone and lighting stayed locked.
![Adjacent boundary keyframes that anchor neighbouring LTX tiles](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/boundary-keys.jpg)
![One LTX-2.3 performance tile, six frames across its 13.4 seconds](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/ltx-tile-contact.jpg)
Each tile ran through a two-stage ComfyUI graph: LTX-2.3 22B at 960x544 with static-camera and dynamic LoRAs, then the LTX spatial upscaler and a detailer LoRA refining to 1920x1088.
## Invisible Joins

Cross-dissolving the tiles would have ghosted the face at every join. Instead, each of the 27 joins is repaired with full-resolution, bidirectional RAFT-Large optical flow over 36 frames (85% flow warp, 15% dissolve) on CUDA. The result is a single continuous 6,660-frame performance, and that file is the only moving source the 3D stage is allowed to see, so no editorial seam can leak into the geometry.
## From Video To Points

Pi3X, run through the Vista4D tooling in WSL, estimates per-frame depth and camera motion from the performance, with SAM3 masks isolating the singer. The song was solved as 111 overlapping 81-frame windows, and 27 of them are centred on the LTX joins so that no reconstruction boundary ever lands on an editorial one.

Pi3X gives depth, cameras and masks, not a finished image. Custom PyTorch and CUDA code turns the visible surface into points coloured by the LTX frames, using three persistent, ordered sub-lattices. Points never re-sample randomly from frame to frame, which removed an early shimmer and gave the film its woven, screen-printed texture.
![The same moment as the LTX-2.3 performance (left) and the final point render (right)](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/ltx-vs-points.jpg)
::video[Same ten seconds: LTX-2.3 performance and final point render, with the master audio](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/ltx-vs-points.mp4)
## Face, Hair And Volume

Monocular depth only knows the side of her that the camera saw. MediaPipe's 478-landmark face track adds real relief to the front of the face, a geometry-bound treatment keeps the pink rabbit mask attached to that surface, and extra layers derived from the silhouette give the body thickness. A separate hair-coloured particle shell carries the silhouette when the camera travels behind her.
![Profile of the reconstructed point volume](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/profile-volume.jpg)
![Rear view: hair-coloured point shell during a turn](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/rear-points.jpg)

This is the honest limit of the method. It is 2.5D reconstruction plus procedural volume, not a full 3D scan of a performer, so the most extreme angles are reserved for fast, energetic moments where the music carries the move.
## A Camera That Listens

From the master mix I extracted 24 fps control curves: energy, accents, impacts, expansion hits, hair gusts and camera hits, across 345 detected musical events, 138 of them strong. Those curves drive point expansion, hair motion and handheld energy, and they decide when the camera commits: calm front and three-quarter dwells in the soft sections; partial arcs, intimate push-ins and occasional full rotations when the song opens up. Her face stays near frame centre through all of it.
![Side view as the camera arcs around the singer](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/side-hair.jpg)
![Camera behind the singer during a full rotation](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/behind-the-head.jpg)
## The Heart Network

Behind her, a 3D network grows out of the performance: small hearts, broken hearts, tags, radar echoes and travelling light packets that follow hidden routes through space. The connecting lines stay invisible, so only the signals moving along them read. The film opens with the singer assembling from falling points and ends with the inverse dissolve.
![Matrix-style point construction at the start of the film](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/matrix-build.jpg)
![Wide shot with the heart and radar network behind the performer](assets/projects/f1r-live-video/network-wide.jpg)
## Directing An Agent

I built this with Codex as the production agent. It wrote and ran the ComfyUI, PyTorch and CUDA tooling and kept a strict ledger of every version, while I made the creative calls: which routes to kill, which look to lock and when a take was good enough. Every approved state was frozen with its manifest and hashes, so a later experiment could never silently overwrite a good version. That discipline is what made 90-odd iterations manageable.
The final 16:9 master is 1920x1080 at 24 fps, composited on CUDA and encoded with NVENC. A native 9:16 version was rendered separately from the same 3D data for social, rather than cropped.
## What I Learned

Generative video gets far more interesting when it stops being the final image and becomes raw material: a performance you can reconstruct, re-light and re-shoot with a camera that did not exist when the clip was made. The hard part was never one model. It was continuity: tiles, joins, reconstruction windows and camera moves all have to agree for 4 minutes 37 seconds.

title: Dark Forest
role: ANIMATED BLENDER SHOT / GENERATED ASSETS + MOTION / LOOK DEVELOPMENT
description: An art-directable animated Blender shot built entirely through conversation with Codex: generated character, props, forest and motion, painted shading and layered lantern light, plus an illustrated 2D look pass.

videos.title: Dark Forest, final shot (28 seconds, with sound)

body: ## Human + Codex + Astra

Dark Forest is a fully art-directable, animated Blender shot: a small traveller carries a lantern down a forest path while something in the dark watches him. I built it without touching Blender myself. My only interface was a conversation with Codex, running OpenAI's Astra model, which generated the assets, rigged and animated the character, assembled the forest and rendered every iteration while I directed the look, the performance and the light.
The result is not a flat AI video. It is an editable 3D scene: every asset, the rig, the camera and the lights can still be changed and re-rendered.
::video[The process in 45 seconds: assets, rig, motion, assembly, light](assets/projects/dark-forest/process-in-45s.mp4)
## Visual Direction

The target was a painted anime look: expressive brushwork, simplified shapes, cool forest shadows and warm lantern light. ImageGen concept frames fixed the mood, palette and composition before any geometry existed, and the same frame became the reference for the final shot's first frame.
![Visual direction concept for the opening frame](assets/projects/dark-forest/direction-concept.webp)
## A Generated Character

The traveller started as a character sheet: front, side, back and three-quarter views with fixed proportions. Four matching views went into Hunyuan3D 3.1, which produced a textured mesh. In Blender he gained real-world scale, a fitted skeleton, skinning and pose corrections for the shoulders, arms and hands that carry the lantern.
![Character sheet used to generate the traveller](assets/projects/dark-forest/character-sheet.jpg)

The backpack and lantern were generated the same way and fitted to him: the straps follow the rig, the lantern's glow and painted surface move with his hand, and the final finger grip was authored in Blender. Every asset in the shot can be turned around below. These are the actual painted scene assets, not concept images.
::embed[turntables]
## Directed Motion

The performance is generated too, with Kimodo, a 3D generative animation model, on the fitted rig. I directed the beats: walk, slow down, turn all the way back, hold, continue. Timing, glances and the lantern carry were adjusted take by take.
::video[Generated 3D walk: character view above, full travel distance below](assets/projects/dark-forest/generated-walk.mp4)

The walk was the hardest part to get right. Early takes were robotic; later ones swayed too much; manually damping the hips broke the gait. What finally worked was fewer constraints rather than more: a handful of root waypoints and no forced footfalls, so the model could find a natural, slightly anxious walk on its own.
## Building The Forest

The forest around the path is assembled from generated conifers, boulders, ferns, a gnarled stump and a broken hollow trunk, all Hunyuan3D meshes built from ImageGen views. Editable terrain gives the path a real slope, and more than 21,000 scattered instances across nine Geometry Nodes layers fill the undergrowth. Six small forest spirits, procedural Blender geometry with glowing eyes, independent blinks and head turns, watch from behind the boulder banks.
::video[Inside the actual Blender scene: moving through the set and repositioning the boy](assets/projects/dark-forest/blender-scene-recording.mp4)
## Painted Surfaces And Light

The textured meshes gained stylised shading and surface-following brushstrokes made with Blender Studio's Brushstroke Tools. Lighting was built in layers: forest fill, then moonlight, then the lantern. Drag through the same first-frame camera from wireframe and white clay to the finished painted, lantern-lit frame.
::embed[breakdown]

Getting there took 60 look versions. The moonlight was approved as "perfect" at one version while the lantern still read as flat; later passes gave the lantern a real falloff gradient, cut the moonlight by 30% and darkened the forest until the lantern became the only warm thing in the frame.
## The Final Shot

The finished shot runs 28 seconds in Eevee: a smooth 24 fps camera with subtle handheld drift, while the character and the rest of the scene animate on twos, at 12 held poses per second, for a hand-animated cadence. Wind moves through branches and plants with delayed responses, and the spirits blink out of sync in the background.
![Frame one of the final shot](assets/projects/dark-forest/cover.jpg)
## An Illustrated Look

The same world also went through a second, flatter look development pass. Concept work defined the valley with a castle on the far ridge, the ascent path and the watchful forest, then tested colour-manga and ink-and-gouache treatments.
![Valley with the castle on the ridge](assets/projects/dark-forest/2d-concept-valley.webp)
![Ink and gouache style study](assets/projects/dark-forest/2d-concept-ink.webp)

For this direction the forest elements were redrawn as painted, cardboard-like cutouts and placed at different depths around real terrain and the animated boy. It reads as 2D, but the camera still has real space to move. The optimised scene saves at 92 MB, and sampled 480p Eevee frames rendered in under a second each on my workstation, light enough to iterate quickly.
![Illustrated conifer cutouts](assets/projects/dark-forest/2d-ink-cards.webp)
![Assembled Blender frame with the illustrated cutouts](assets/projects/dark-forest/2d-blender-scene.webp)
::video[Two-shot Blender edit with the illustrated forest, with sound](assets/projects/dark-forest/look-dev-blender-edit.mp4)
## Pushing The Ink With AI Video

Finally I used AI video to push the drawn look further. An approved ImageGen ink drawing of the opening served as the guide frame, the boy as the only image reference, and DepthCrafter depth from the Blender shot as the motion control, generated with MiniMax H3 in ComfyUI and refined in a second pass. When the second shot's contours came out soft, the fix went into the source drawing rather than sharpening the video.
![Approved ink direction for the opening](assets/projects/dark-forest/2d-manga-opening.webp)
::video[Two-shot ink edit, generated from the Blender shots](assets/projects/dark-forest/look-dev-ink-edit.mp4)
## What I Learned

Directing through conversation works when everything stays editable. Generated meshes, generated motion and generated light are only useful if you can still grab one and change it, and a Blender scene keeps that possible. The craft moved from operating tools to judging takes: knowing which walk felt afraid, which light was too flat, and when a version was finally right.
The full interactive making-of, with scroll-driven breakdowns and every turntable, lives at [darkforest3d.pages.dev](https://darkforest3d.pages.dev/).

title: Cat Walkman
description: AI illustration experiment built with SDXL and ControlNet workflows, with music created in Suno.
body: ## Process Notes

I made this image in Invoke while experimenting with SDXL models and ControlNets. The main idea was to keep the generated image under direction instead of just letting the model improvise: block the composition, steer the shapes with control inputs, iterate the prompt and model response, then keep pushing the frame until the illustration felt like a finished cover image rather than a raw generation.

The making-of video shows that the image is built through iteration: composition first, then detail passes, cleanup, and final mood. I also made the music in Suno, so the project became a small AI illustration and music experiment rather than only a still image.

title: Daft Punk cover art
description: AI-driven cover-art workflow using ComfyUI, SDXL, posing tools, and Photoshop cleanup for multi-character direction.

videos.title: Making of Daft Punk ComfyUI Illustration

body: ## Process Notes

I used ComfyUI and SDXL to build a controlled cover-art workflow with multiple elements and characters. The main challenge was not just generating one nice frame; it was directing the scene: posing the characters, keeping the two figures readable, mixing the car/environment/helmet shapes together, and then upscaling the result without losing the cover-art composition.

For the character pose pass I used Reallusion Character Creator to create OpenPose ControlNet skeletons. Photoshop came in for small positional edits and cleanup early in the process, while ComfyUI handled the heavier image generation, mixing, refinement, and upscale steps. The result is an AI cover-art workflow where I still keep authorial control over staging and direction.

title: trips
description: AI environment experiment where I pushed current models and services to see how much quality I could get from strange alien-world drone footage.
body: ## Project Notes

I was playing with AI workflows to see how much quality I could squeeze out of the models and services available at the time. The goal was to create drone-like footage from a strange alien planet: unfamiliar, but still close enough to Earth that the environments feel physically readable.
The still images were generated in ComfyUI with Flux and upscaled there as well. I used those stills as starting frames in Runway, made the music with Aiva, and edited the final video in Blender.

title: TAVI Medical Animation
role: MEDICAL ANIMATION / MODELLING, RIGGING, ANIMATION, LOOK DEVELOPMENT, COMPOSITING
description: An 80-second patient-education film of a transcatheter aortic valve implantation, made at and for Medify: one Blender scene and one camera from the standing patient to the new valve working inside a cutaway heart.

videos.title: TAVI, the full film (80 seconds, silent)

body: ## The Brief

TAVI, transcatheter aortic valve implantation, replaces a failing aortic valve without opening the chest. A new valve is crimped onto a balloon, threaded up from the groin through the femoral artery and the aorta, and expanded inside the old valve. This film explains that procedure to the patient who is about to have it, in 80 seconds.

I made it at Medify in 2022 and did all of it myself: the patient, the theatre, the heart, the device, the animation, the look, the render layers and the final comp. It is one of a long series of animated procedures I built there, and the heart from this film went on to carry more than fifteen other cardiac procedures.
![The diseased aortic valve from above, early in the film](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/still-diseased-valve.webp)
## One Scene, One Camera

The whole film is a single Blender scene with a single animated camera: 2,000 frames at 25 fps, rendered in Eevee at 1920 by 1440. There are no cuts between files. The camera starts on the standing patient, dives through the chest to the valve, pulls back out to the operating table, follows the catheter up the aorta and ends inside the cutaway heart. Every dissolve in the film is a blend between render layers of the same frame.

For this page I went back into that scene four years later. Everything below that is not the film itself was rendered fresh from the original file in Blender 3.3, the version the film was rendered with.
## The Patient

The patient is a Character Creator figure on a 101-bone rig. His job is to make the viewer feel that this is about a person before the camera goes inside. The gown builds onto him beside the table, he sits, swings his legs up and lies back, and a drape covers his legs. The gown and the drape are cloth simulations that follow the body through that whole move.
::video[Patient and theatre: clay render from the film camera beside the finished film](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/patient-clay-vs-final.mp4)
![On the table, before the camera goes in](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/still-patient-table.webp)
## The Heart

The heart exists twice in the scene. One version is whole, with coronary arteries and veins on its surface. The other is cut open along the long axis to show the chambers, the chordae and the valves. Both follow the patient's body and the same heartbeat, so they can be dissolved into each other at any frame. The valves are separate meshes with their own beat cycle, so the aortic valve can be shown on its own, opening and closing, with nothing in front of it.

Turn the assets around below: the whole heart, the cutaway, the replacement valve on its balloon and the valve after it has been expanded. The clay versions show the modelling without the painted textures.
::embed[turntables]
## The Valve

The replacement valve is a stent frame with a fabric skirt and three leaflets. It has three shapes blended over time: crimped on the balloon, expanded by it, and working on its own, opening and closing with the heartbeat. The balloon and the valve both follow a curve that runs from the groin to the aortic root, so the whole delivery is animated by sliding them along one path. The guide wire and the catheters are drawn along the same family of curves.
The film watches the deployment from a distance, through the heart wall. This is the same animation from a new camera, close on the valve, with only the valve layer switched on.
::video[A new close-up of the deployment: balloon in, valve expanded, old leaflets pushed aside, new leaflets working](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/valve-close-up.mp4)
## Deployment

Here is the centre of the film as geometry and as the finished picture. On the left, the cutaway heart is ghosted so the valve, the balloon and the wires stay readable. On the right is the same stretch of the film.
::video[Deployment: clay render of the heart and device layers beside the finished film](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/deployment-clay-vs-final.mp4)
## Built In Layers

The scene renders as six layers through the same camera: the whole heart with its vessels, the cutaway heart, the valves and device, the instruments, the contrast dye and the patient. Each one carries ambient occlusion, a gloss pass and object mattes. The final picture was assembled from those layers in After Effects: the ghosted outer heart over the cutaway, the glow around the aortic root and the grade all happen there.
Drag through one frame of the deployment: the whole heart, the cutaway, the device placed inside it and the finished frame from the film.
::embed[breakdown]
The contrast dye at the aortic root is a small smoke simulation, emitted at the tip of its own catheter and rendered as a separate layer so its strength could be set in the comp.
## Frames From The Film
![The cutaway reveal as the catheter arrives](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/still-cutaway-reveal.webp)
![The new valve in place inside the old one](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/still-valve-deployed.webp)
![The new valve from above, opening with the heartbeat](assets/projects/tavi-medical-animation/still-new-valve.webp)
